- If sentiment is consistently positive (≥0.6) and forecast is rising steadily, reduce slope to avoid over-optimism; true outcomes often peak then drop.
- If sentiment is negative (≤0.3) and forecast is flat or rising, increase downward bias — true outcomes frequently rebound after dips.
- After a sharp spike in price (e.g., >75), forecast tends to overshoot; cap next 3–5 periods at +2–3% above peak to avoid overcorrection.
- When sentiment is high (≥0.7) and price is trending up, model often overestimates; apply 1–2% downward adjustment to avoid mean reversion bias.
- If forecast is flat or slightly rising while sentiment is low (≤0.4), true outcome often dips — add 1–3% downward bias to avoid lagged overconfidence.
- For 30-day horizon, if last 3–5 days show strong mean reversion (e.g., 3 consecutive drops), forecast should be adjusted downward by 1–2% to reflect momentum correction.
- If sentiment is volatile (alternating 0.2–0.8) and forecast is smooth, introduce 1–2% volatility buffer to account for sentiment-driven noise.
